questions.text: A METAR reports: FEW012 SCT025 BKN060. What is the ceiling, and how should the height be interpreted?

options.label: A
options.text: The ceiling is the FEW012 layer at 1,200 feet MSL because the ceiling is defined as the lowest cloud layer regardless of coverage category

options.label: B
options.text: The ceiling is the BKN060 layer at 6,000 feet AGL because the ceiling is the lowest broken or overcast layer, and all METAR sky condition heights are reported in AGL

options.label: C
options.text: The ceiling is the SCT025 layer at 2,500 feet MSL because scattered coverage represents the meteorological threshold at which clouds affect VFR flight planning

options.label: D
options.text: There is no ceiling because BKN coverage at 6,000 feet AGL does not affect VFR operations, and a ceiling only exists when the OVC designation appears in the sky condition group

questions.explanation: In aviation meteorology, the ceiling is defined as the height above the earth's surface of the lowest layer of clouds or obscuring phenomena that is reported as broken (BKN) or overcast (OVC). The FEW (1/8–2/8) and SCT (3/8–4/8) layers do not constitute a ceiling. The BKN060 layer at 6,000 AGL is the ceiling. All METAR sky condition heights are reported in HUNDREDS of feet ABOVE GROUND LEVEL — not MSL. The DPE will listen specifically for 'AGL' when the applicant reads a METAR sky condition group. This airport is VFR (ceiling above 3,000 AGL and no visibility restriction reported).

questions.text: A METAR reports: 18015KT. The airport's magnetic variation is 8°E. What is the equivalent magnetic wind direction a pilot should use when selecting a runway?

options.label: A
options.text: 180° magnetic — METAR wind directions are already stated in magnetic degrees to align with runway headings and require no variation correction for runway selection

options.label: B
options.text: 172° magnetic — METAR text reports state wind in True degrees; to convert to magnetic, subtract easterly variation: 180° - 8° = 172° magnetic

options.label: C
options.text: 188° magnetic — METAR text reports state wind in True degrees; to convert to magnetic, add easterly variation: 180° + 8° = 188° magnetic

options.label: D
options.text: 180° magnetic — airport runways are designated in true degrees and no variation correction is needed when selecting a runway from METAR wind data

questions.explanation: METAR text reports state wind direction relative to TRUE NORTH. To convert True direction to Magnetic, the rule is: East variation is subtracted; West variation is added. (Memory aid: East is Least, West is Best.) With an 8°E variation: 180° True - 8° = 172° Magnetic. Runway numbers are based on magnetic headings — runway 17 (170° magnetic) or runway 18 (180° magnetic) would be the best landing options. This true-to-magnetic conversion is one of the most frequently missed METAR questions on the oral exam because pilots often assume the METAR is already in magnetic. Voice ATIS broadcasts, by contrast, already convert wind to magnetic.

questions.text: A pilot decodes the following METAR element: 'M02/M08.' What do these values represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Temperature 2°C and dewpoint 8°C with the M prefix indicating the values are measured in Metric format rather than the Fahrenheit format used in US weather reports

options.label: B
options.text: Temperature -2°C and dewpoint -8°C with the M prefix indicating 'minus'; the dewpoint is lower than the temperature, indicating very dry air at this station

options.label: C
options.text: Temperature -2°F and dewpoint -8°F with the M prefix converting the standard METAR Celsius scale to Fahrenheit for stations in the contiguous United States above 3,000 feet MSL

options.label: D
options.text: Temperature missing and dewpoint missing, where M is a placeholder code indicating the ASOS sensor malfunctioned and the values are not available for this observation cycle

questions.explanation: In METAR format, the 'M' prefix before a temperature or dewpoint value stands for 'Minus' — indicating a negative (below freezing) value. M02/M08 means Temperature -2°C and Dewpoint -8°C. Since temperatures are always in Celsius in METARs worldwide, there is no Fahrenheit conversion in standard aviation weather products. The temperature-dewpoint spread (6°C in this case) indicates relatively dry air and a low probability of visible moisture-related phenomena at this station, though both values are below freezing, indicating structural ice risk in any visible moisture at altitude.

questions.text: A METAR at 1400Z reports VFR conditions with a ceiling of 3,500 AGL. A pilot plans to arrive at 1440Z. At 1410Z, a SPECI is issued. Which condition most likely triggered the SPECI?

options.label: A
options.text: A moderate wind shift of 20 degrees from northwest to north, which is the minimum angular change required to trigger SPECI issuance regardless of wind speed

options.label: B
options.text: The temperature dropping 2°C in 10 minutes, which automatically triggers a SPECI when ambient temperatures approach the freezing level at any altitude

options.label: C
options.text: The ceiling dropping from 3,500 AGL to below 3,000 AGL, crossing the VFR-to-MVFR threshold — one of the defined trigger conditions for an off-cycle SPECI report

options.label: D
options.text: The automatic station completing its off-cycle calibration cycle, which triggers a SPECI every 10 minutes regardless of atmospheric change as a routine maintenance notification

questions.explanation: SPECI reports are issued when conditions change rapidly and cross defined meteorological thresholds before the next routine METAR. Ceiling thresholds that trigger SPECI issuance include: drops below 3,000 feet AGL (VFR to MVFR boundary), drops below 1,500 AGL, drops below 1,000 AGL, or drops below 500 AGL. A ceiling falling from 3,500 to below 3,000 AGL crosses the first SPECI trigger threshold. Option A incorrectly states 20 degrees as the wind shift trigger — the actual trigger for wind shift is 45 degrees or more with the new wind speed of 10 knots or greater. Option D invents an automatic calibration trigger that does not exist in METAR/SPECI operational procedures.

questions.text: A METAR reads: 0900Z, OVC004, visibility 1/2SM FG. What is the flight category for this airport?

options.label: A
options.text: IFR — a ceiling of 400 AGL and visibility of 1/2SM both fall within the IFR category (ceiling 500–999 AGL or visibility 1–3SM), making this a significant but not extreme weather situation

options.label: B
options.text: MVFR — the overcast ceiling at 400 AGL qualifies as marginal visual flight rules, which applies whenever the ceiling drops below 1,000 AGL regardless of the associated visibility conditions

options.label: C
options.text: LIFR — an overcast ceiling of 400 AGL (below 500 AGL) and visibility of 1/2SM (below 1SM) both satisfy the Low IFR flight category, the most restrictive designation in the system

options.label: D
options.text: VFR — the FG code in the METAR is an advisory notation only; fog does not legally affect the VFR flight category determination, which is based solely on cloud ceiling height

questions.explanation: LIFR (Low IFR) is the most restrictive flight category and applies when the ceiling is below 500 feet AGL OR visibility is below 1 statute mile. In this METAR, BOTH conditions are LIFR: OVC004 = overcast at 400 AGL (below the 500 AGL LIFR threshold) AND visibility 1/2SM FG = half a statute mile in fog (below the 1SM LIFR threshold). Either condition alone would qualify as LIFR; both together represent the worst possible surface conditions for flight. Option A (IFR) is a partial answer — the conditions are worse than standard IFR. Option B (MVFR) significantly understates the severity. Option D is entirely incorrect — visibility restrictions from fog directly determine flight category.

questions.text: A METAR sky condition reads: 'CLR.' The pilot is flying toward this station. What does CLR specifically mean on an automated surface observing system?

options.label: A
options.text: Clear sky — no clouds exist anywhere in the vicinity of the station, as confirmed by both the automated sensors and the human meteorological observers on duty at the station

options.label: B
options.text: No clouds detected below 12,000 feet AGL by the automated sensor — clouds may exist above 12,000 AGL or outside the narrow vertical field of view of the ASOS optical sensor

options.label: C
options.text: Clear below 6,500 feet AGL only — ASOS stations automatically transition to SKC reporting above 6,500 feet because sensor accuracy degrades at higher altitudes

options.label: D
options.text: Sky condition cannot be reported — CLR is a maintenance code indicating the cloud sensor has malfunctioned and ceiling data is temporarily unavailable for this observation

questions.explanation: CLR is the code used by automated observing systems (ASOS/AWOS) when no clouds are detected below 12,000 feet AGL. The critical limitation: ASOS cloud sensors only look straight up within a very narrow vertical cone and only detect layers up to 12,000 AGL. A pilot approaching this station could have unlimited visibility and a CLR sky below 12,000 AGL while massive thunderstorm anvils at 40,000 feet are building 10 miles to the west — completely invisible to the sensor. SKC (sky clear) is used by human observers to indicate clear skies with no uncertainty limitation, reflecting actual visual observation of the sky dome. The CLR-vs-SKC distinction matters most when the METAR source is an automated unattended station.

questions.text: You check the 1400Z METAR before departure. It shows VFR with a 2,500 AGL broken ceiling. Your destination is 90 minutes away and you plan to arrive at 1530Z. No SPECI has been issued yet. During your flight at 1445Z, you encounter a rapidly developing overcast layer descending quickly. What is the SAFEST response?

options.label: A
options.text: Continue toward the destination — the 1400Z METAR is the most current official report, and no SPECI means conditions have not changed enough to trigger an advisory; conditions may improve as a front moves through

options.label: B
options.text: Request an in-flight weather update from FSS or Approach Control for the destination, evaluate updated conditions, and divert immediately if conditions are at or below your personal minimums rather than pressing toward an unknown ceiling

options.label: C
options.text: Descend below the developing overcast layer and continue VFR regardless of altitude — maintaining visual contact with the ground is always legal and safe under VFR flight rules in uncontrolled airspace

options.label: D
options.text: Immediately perform a 180-degree turn and return to departure airport without requesting any weather update — any developing overcast layer automatically means the destination is IFR and no further evaluation is needed

questions.explanation: The absence of a SPECI does not mean conditions have not changed — SPECI triggers are based on specific threshold crossing values, and rapidly developing weather may not yet have crossed a reporting threshold. The correct action is to proactively obtain an in-flight update through FSS (on 122.2 MHz) or the nearest approach control, assess the current destination METAR or PIREPs, and make a data-driven divert-or-continue decision. Option A is Invulnerability — trusting a 45-minute-old METAR in rapidly changing conditions. Option C is Macho — descending to chase the floor of an overcast layer risks entering IMC at low altitude in terrain. NTSB controlled-flight-into-terrain (CFIT) statistics consistently implicate this exact behavior. Option D is Resignation — an overcast layer 90 miles from the destination is not sufficient information to declare the destination IFR without seeking current data.
questions.sjt_rationale: Option A is Invulnerability — relying on stale data in observed changing conditions. Option C is Macho — pressing into degrading conditions by descending under the weather. Option D is Resignation — an overreaction that abandons information-gathering before deciding. Option B is the professionally correct response: gather current data, then decide.

questions.text: During a checkride oral, the DPE hands you a METAR and asks you to decode it completely. You decode all elements correctly but when you read 'SCT028' you say '2,800 feet MSL.' The DPE says nothing and waits. What is the correct action?

options.label: A
options.text: Stand by your answer — METAR cloud heights are stated relative to the station elevation which is approximated by MSL, and 2,800 feet MSL is a reasonable interpretation for a sea-level airport

options.label: B
options.text: Self-correct immediately: 'I apologize — METAR sky condition heights are reported in hundreds of feet above ground level, not MSL. SCT028 means scattered clouds at 2,800 feet AGL.'

options.label: C
options.text: Wait for the DPE to correct you — it is the examiner's responsibility to identify errors on a practical test, and responding to ambiguous DPE silence by self-correcting may suggest the applicant lacked initial confidence

options.label: D
options.text: Add that 2,800 feet MSL and AGL are equivalent at sea-level airports and the distinction is only operationally relevant at high-elevation airports in the western United States

questions.explanation: The DPE's silence is a deliberate evaluative pause — not confirmation that the answer was correct. The applicant who immediately recognizes and self-corrects the AGL error demonstrates exactly the self-monitoring and error-correction skills that define safe aeronautical decision-making. METAR sky condition heights are ALWAYS in AGL — this is universal to all METAR products worldwide, not limited to MSL-equivalent airports. Option A is Macho — defending an error by adding an incorrect qualifier rather than acknowledging the mistake. Option C is Resignation — abdicating self-monitoring responsibility. Option D is a compounded error — the MSL/AGL distinction is critically important at ALL airports because AGL heights directly determine safe approach altitudes and obstacle clearance regardless of field elevation.
questions.sjt_rationale: Option A is Macho — defending an incorrect answer with false certainty. Option C is Resignation — waiting for someone else to identify your own error. Option D compounds the Macho rationalization with a second factual error. Option B demonstrates professional competence through immediate self-correction.
